subject: biology
title: Dihybrid crosses, linkage, epistasis and chi-squared
key_idea: A dihybrid cross follows two genes at once. Independent genes give a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio, and linkage or epistasis changes that ratio. Sex-linked genes lie on the X chromosome. The chi-squared test decides whether observed results fit the ratio expected.

blocks.text: A dihybrid cross follows two genes on different chromosomes. The genes are inherited independently, because homologous pairs line up and separate at random in meiosis.

items: Each parent makes four types of gamete when heterozygous at both loci.
For RrYy the gametes are RY, Ry, rY and ry, in equal numbers.
Use a 4 × 4 Punnett square, giving 16 combinations.
RrYy × RrYy gives 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green.

blocks.text: In this example R is round and Y is yellow, and both are dominant.

rows: All RrYy, then 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 in the next generation

items: Two heterozygous parents give 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 when the genes are on different chromosomes.
A dihybrid test cross gives 1 : 1 : 1 : 1.
Write out every gamete before filling in the square.

blocks.text: A **sex-linked** gene is on a sex chromosome, usually the X. The Y chromosome carries very few of the same genes.

items: Females are XX and have two alleles. Males are XY and have only one allele for an X-linked gene.
A recessive X-linked allele shows in every male who has it, because there is no second allele to mask it.
A female shows the trait only if she has two copies. A heterozygous female is a carrier.
A father passes his X to his daughters and his Y to his sons, so he never passes an X-linked allele to a son.
Haemophilia and red-green colour blindness are X-linked recessive conditions.

blocks.text: In the cross below, Xᴴ is the normal allele and Xʰ is the recessive allele. Pick a mother and a father.

diagram.alt: A predictor for an X-linked recessive condition. Pick the parents and see the daughters, the sons and the chance that a child is affected.

items: Males have one X, so one recessive allele is enough to show the trait.
Sons get their X from their mother only.
More males than females are affected by X-linked recessive conditions.

blocks.text: Genes on the same autosome are **linked**. They are on the same chromosome, so they are inherited together.

items: A heterozygote with alleles A and B on one chromosome and a and b on the other makes mostly AB and ab gametes. These are the parental types.
Crossing over between the two loci in prophase I makes a few Ab and aB gametes. These are the recombinants.
In a test cross, the parental phenotypes are far more common than the recombinant phenotypes.
The closer two loci are, the less often crossing over separates them, so the fewer recombinants there are.

blocks.text: A ratio of offspring that is not 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 in a test cross, with two phenotypes much more common than the other two, points to linkage.

items: Linked genes are on the same chromosome and are inherited together.
Crossing over makes the few recombinant offspring.
Two common phenotypes and two rare ones suggest linkage.

blocks.text: In **epistasis**, an allele at one locus affects or masks the expression of alleles at a second locus. The two genes may be on different chromosomes, but they do not act separately.

items: Example: in mice, gene C makes pigment and gene A decides the pattern of colour.
A mouse with genotype cc makes no pigment, so it is albino whatever alleles it has at the A locus.
A cross of two heterozygotes (AaCc × AaCc) gives 9 agouti : 3 black : 4 albino, instead of 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
The 16 combinations still add up, but the albino classes look the same, so fewer phenotypes appear.

blocks.text: Other epistatic crosses give ratios such as 9 : 7 or 12 : 3 : 1. A modified ratio that still totals 16 suggests epistasis.

items: Epistasis: one gene masks or modifies the expression of another.
The ratio is a modified version of 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, still adding to 16.
Always work out the genotypes with a Punnett square before naming the phenotypes.

blocks.text: Real results never match the expected ratio exactly. The chi-squared test checks whether the difference is just chance.

items.text: State that there is no significant difference between the observed and expected results.
Share the total in the expected ratio. For 3 : 1 and 160 offspring, expect 120 and 40.
Use the formula below, for every class, and add the answers.
Find the critical value at probability 0.05 (5%) in the table you are given.

blocks.label: Chi-squared
where: O = observed number in a class
E = expected number in that class
Σ = the sum over all classes

items: If χ² is **greater than** the critical value, reject the null hypothesis. The difference is significant: it is unlikely (less than 5%) to be due to chance alone.
If χ² is **less than** the critical value, accept the null hypothesis. The difference is not significant and could be due to chance.
Use counts, never percentages, in the formula.

blocks.text: Try one with new numbers. A 3 : 1 ratio has two classes, so there is 1 degree of freedom.

diagram.alt: A chi-squared practice question with new numbers each time, for an expected 3 : 1 ratio.
diagram.question: A cross is expected to give a 3 : 1 ratio. The observed offspring are {a} with the dominant phenotype and {b} with the recessive phenotype. Calculate χ² to 2 decimal places.
working: Total = {a} + {b}. Expected dominant = three quarters of the total. Expected recessive = one quarter of the total.
For each class, work out (O − E)² ÷ E.
Degrees of freedom = 1. Compare with the critical value 3.84 at p = 0.05.

items: Null hypothesis: no significant difference between observed and expected.
χ² greater than the critical value at 0.05: reject the null hypothesis.
Degrees of freedom = number of classes − 1.

checks.q: Two plants heterozygous for two independent genes are crossed. State the expected phenotype ratio of the offspring.
checks.a: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 (two dominant features : one dominant, one recessive : the other dominant, recessive : both recessive).

checks.q: A woman is a carrier of haemophilia, an X-linked recessive condition. Her partner is unaffected. Explain why their sons are more likely than their daughters to be affected.
checks.a: The mother passes on either the Xʰ allele or the Xᴴ allele, each with probability one half. A son gets his X only from his mother, and has no second X to mask a recessive allele, so half the sons are affected. A daughter also gets the father's Xᴴ, which masks the recessive allele, so she is unaffected, though she may be a carrier.

checks.q: A student expects a 3 : 1 ratio and gets 84 dominant and 36 recessive offspring. χ² = 1.6. The critical value is 3.84 at p = 0.05. State and explain the conclusion.
checks.a: Degrees of freedom = 1. χ² (1.6) is less than 3.84, so the null hypothesis is accepted. There is no significant difference between observed and expected results; the difference is likely due to chance.

blocks.text: A locus (plural loci) is the location of a gene on a chromosome. You need to link loci to linkage and sex linkage.

items: Linked genes are at different loci on the same chromosome, so they stay together unless crossing over separates them.
In sex linkage the locus is on a sex chromosome, so the inheritance pattern differs between males and females.
Recombinant gametes from linked loci are always fewer than parental types when the loci are close.
You must construct genetic diagrams for dihybrid crosses with autosomal linkage and with epistasis.
You do not need to learn the expected ratios for the different types of epistasis. Work them out from the genotypes in the question.
The formula for χ² is provided in the exam.

Use phenotypic ratios to identify the pattern: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 suggests independent genes, two common and two rare classes suggest linkage, and fewer than four phenotype classes that still total 16 parts suggest epistasis.
Genetic diagrams must cover monogenic inheritance, dihybrid inheritance, multiple alleles, sex linkage and codominance.
The formula χ² = Σ (fₒ − fₑ)² ÷ fₑ is provided. Here fₒ is the observed frequency and fₑ the expected frequency.
